Lessons.Title: Exploring Circles
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Identify center, radius, diameter and circumference, and use the equal-distance definition of a circle. First-party mathematical examples, referencing the historical OUR/IM source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/3/2/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 lineage; no publisher artwork).

This lesson distinguishes its intended measurement, model and units. Work through the exact examples and explain how the representation supports each conclusion. Official OUR/IM 2017–2019 student task alignment: Recognizing circles; Drawing Circles; Identifying Radii and Diameters. This lesson requires students to Build a first-party circle with compass and mark multiple equal-distance points, radii, and a diameter. KeyConcepts.Title: Circle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A circle consists of points in a plane at equal distance from one center.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distance from the center to every point on a circle is r.
KeyConcepts.Example: Points 5 units from center O lie on the circle of radius 5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Radius and diameter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Radius connects center to circle; diameter crosses the center from edge to edge.
KeyConcepts.Example: r=4 cm gives d=8 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Circumference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Circumference is distance once around the circular boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: It is a length, not an area.
KeyConcepts.Example: A circular hoop's rim is measured in cm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert radius to diameter
WorkedExamples.Question: A circle has radius 4.5 cm. Find its diameter.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Half of 9 is 4.5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify a circle
WorkedExamples.Question: Are all points exactly 3 cm from point O on the same circle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
Steps: Check that every candidate point has distance 3 cm.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, their locus is a circle of radius 3 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Interior points are not on the boundary unless exactly 3 cm away.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find radius
WorkedExamples.Question: A circle's diameter is 18 mm. Find radius.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Recognizing circles
WorkedExamples.Question: A student draws a circle centered O with radius 3 cm. They mark A and B on the circle on opposite sides of O and point C at distance 2 cm from O. Which of A,B,C lie on the circle, what is AB, and why?
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Set the compass opening to 3 cm from O and trace a complete circle.
Measure OA=OB=3 cm; C is inside because OC=2 cm, not 3 cm.
If A,O,B are collinear, AB=OA+OB=6 cm, a diameter.
Exchange the drawing and check equal radii and that the diameter actually passes through O.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A and B lie on the circle; C does not; the diameter AB is 6 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher examines the original compass figure, selected points, center and markings; text arithmetic alone is incomplete.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling diameter a radius
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A diameter spans both sides of the center.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide diameter by two to find radius.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using square units for circumference
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Circumference is a one-dimensional boundary length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Measure it in linear units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the appropriate teacher rubric for the drawing or investigation and treat formula-based auto-marking only as supplementary practice.

SummaryPoints: Distance from the center to every point on a circle is r.
It is a length, not an area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pi
KeyConcepts.Definition: π is the constant ratio of circumference C to diameter d.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional measurements
KeyConcepts.Definition: Circumference and diameter have a zero-intercept proportional relationship.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling d doubles C.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measured approximations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Physical measurements can approximate π with small error.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Estimate C/d rather than expect exact decimals.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 10 cm diameter yields circumference approximately 31.4 cm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute from diameter
WorkedExamples.Question: Find circumference for a 6 cm diameter in terms of π.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: C/d=π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate π
WorkedExamples.Question: A measured diameter is 8 cm and circumference about 25.1 cm. Estimate C/d.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
Steps: Explain a small discrepancy as measurement/rounding error.
WorkedExamples.Check: Close to π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale two circles
WorkedExamples.Question: If diameter increases from 4 to 10 cm, how does circumference change?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Same ratio as diameters.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Circular Objects
WorkedExamples.Question: Three independent measured circles give approximate (d,C) pairs in cm (4.0,12.6),(7.0,22.0),(10.0,31.4). Plot them and explain what C/d suggests and why measured values may vary.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Record original string/ruler measurements to sensible precision and label the units.
Plot the (diameter,circumference) points and compare the approximate straight-line trend through the origin.
Discuss string stretch, imprecise contact and ruler reading as sources of scatter.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The observed ratio C/d is around 3.14, an estimate of π; real measurements may differ.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks a physical collection, measured table, plotted pairs and measurement-error explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating π as exactly 3.14
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 3.14 is an approximation to irrational π.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep π exact when asked.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming C grows by area factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Circumference is a length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the linear scale factor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the appropriate teacher rubric for the drawing or investigation and treat formula-based auto-marking only as supplementary practice.

SummaryPoints: Estimate C/d rather than expect exact decimals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Full circumference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distance around a circle is π times its diameter.
KeyConcepts.Example: r=5 gives 10π.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arc fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A half-circle arc is half its circle circumference.
KeyConcepts.Example: A semicircle of r=4 has arc 4π.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Include all external boundary edges, both straight and curved.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not count internal shared edges.
KeyConcepts.Example: A semicircle attached to a 8-by-5 rectangle replaces one side of length 8 with arc 4π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find circumference
WorkedExamples.Question: Find exact circumference of a radius-7 circle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: A diameter of 14 gives πd=14π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find radius
WorkedExamples.Question: A circle has circumference 18π cm. Find its radius.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Semicircle boundary
WorkedExamples.Question: A semicircular region has radius 3 cm. What is its complete perimeter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both straight and curved external edges are counted.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Applying Circumference to Tracks
WorkedExamples.Question: An original running track has two straight segments of 80 m each and two semicircular turns of radius 20 m. Calculate the inside lap length and make a labeled diagram.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: The two semicircles together make one full circle of radius 20 m, length 2π×20=40π m.
Sketch each semicircle attached to the two straights; do not double-count the joining segments.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies the original shape, correct two-half-circle decomposition and units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Omitting the diameter of a standalone semicircle
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Its perimeter has an arc and a flat edge.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add the diameter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using radius in C=πd without doubling
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The formula uses diameter, not radius.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 2πr when given r.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.

SummaryPoints: Do not count internal shared edges.

KeyConcepts.Title: One revolution
KeyConcepts.Definition: A wheel rolling without slipping travels one circumference per complete turn.
KeyConcepts.Example: d=1 m gives π m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple revolutions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total distance equals revolutions times circumference.
KeyConcepts.Example: 10 turns at diameter 0.5 m gives 5π m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rotational speed
KeyConcepts.Definition: Revolutions per time scale distance per time.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 turns/sec with C=2 m yields 6 m/sec.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distance after turns
WorkedExamples.Question: A wheel has diameter 0.6 m and rotates 20 times without slipping.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare wheels
WorkedExamples.Question: Wheel A diameter 1 m and wheel B diameter 2 m travel the same 10π m. How many turns each?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Larger wheel needs fewer turns.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rotational travel rate
WorkedExamples.Question: A wheel has circumference 1.5 m and spins 4 times per second without slipping. Find speed.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Units simplify correctly.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Rolling Circles
WorkedExamples.Question: A toy wheel has diameter 0.4 m. A taped marker on the rim starts at the floor. Predict travel after 1, 5 and 30 complete forward turns with no slipping, then check a rolling model.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Compute one turn's distance from circumference: C=π×0.4=0.4π m.
For 5 turns calculate 2π m, for 30 turns calculate 12π m.
Mark one full rotation by the rim marker returning to its original orientation; measure distance against the predicted circumference.
Explain that slipping or an uneven rolling surface invalidates the exact distance-per-turn rule.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1 turn 0.4π m, 5 turns 2π m, 30 turns 12π m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the rolling trial, rotation counts, labeled measurement table and explicit no-slip assumption.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using wheel area for travel distance
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Each full turn advances by the boundary length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use circumference, not area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring slip
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Distance per turn equals circumference only when rolling without slipping.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State this modeling assumption.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the appropriate teacher rubric for the drawing or investigation and treat formula-based auto-marking only as supplementary practice.

Visuals.Description: Travel per turn is one circumference of the wheel. Independently authored accessible comparison table with labeled rows and no publisher image.

ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Decompose irregular polygons and estimate uncertain geographic shapes with clearly stated methods and approximations. First-party mathematical examples, referencing the historical OUR/IM source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/3/6/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 lineage; no publisher artwork).

This lesson distinguishes its intended measurement, model and units. Work through the exact examples and explain how the representation supports each conclusion. Official OUR/IM 2017–2019 student task alignment: Estimating Areas of Complex Regions; Estimating Maps with Grid Squares. This lesson requires students to Estimate by decomposition and bounding rectangles without pretending an irregular area is exact. Equivalent first-party learner activity and its drawing/measurement evidence need teacher review; equations and visual tables are supporting representations only. Student source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/3/6/index.html.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decomposition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Split a complex region into standard polygons.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 5×4 rectangle plus 3×2 rectangle gives 26 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Subtraction of cutouts
KeyConcepts.Definition: An irregular region can be a large enclosing shape minus exclusions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Subtract the area of holes or missing corners.
KeyConcepts.Example: 60−12=48 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A grid or polygon fit approximates a nonpolygonal boundary.
KeyConcepts.Example: A count of 30 mostly filled grid squares suggests area near 30 squares.

WorkedExamples.Title: L-shaped floor area
WorkedExamples.Question: A shape combines a 5×4 rectangle and a 3×2 rectangle without overlap. Find area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Parts are disjoint.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cutout region
WorkedExamples.Question: A 9-by-7 rectangle lacks a 3-by-2 corner. Find remaining area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Avoid double counting cutout.

WorkedExamples.Title: Grid estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: A district outline covers 18 full squares and about 8 half-squares on a 1 km² grid. Estimate area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Uncertain boundary coverage makes this an estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Estimating Areas of Complex Regions
WorkedExamples.Question: A student sketches a nonrectangular garden within an 8 m by 6 m bounding rectangle. An identified 2 m by 3 m cutout is definitely outside; the uncertain curved boundary contains between 1 and 3 square meters of additional excluded area. Give a defensible area interval.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Remove the known rectangular cutout 2×3=6 m², leaving 42 m².
The additional excluded irregular portion is between 1 and 3 m².
Therefore the remaining region is between 42−3=39 and 42−1=41 m²; annotate the sketched bounding regions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A defensible estimate is 39–41 m², not an exact 40 m² without more data.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher examines the student's labeled decomposition, uncertainty boundaries and explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding overlapping decomposed pieces
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Overlap is double-counted.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use nonoverlapping subdivisions or subtract intersections.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Presenting a map-based estimate as exact
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Irregular boundaries require approximations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the grid size and uncertainty.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the appropriate teacher rubric for the drawing or investigation and treat formula-based auto-marking only as supplementary practice.

SummaryPoints: Subtract the area of holes or missing corners.

Visuals.Description: Two nonoverlapping rectangles are added to estimate the total covered area. Independently authored accessible comparison table with labeled rows and no publisher image.

Lessons.Title: Exploring the Area of a Circle
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Estimate circular area from grids and squares, and identify why area is not proportional to diameter. First-party mathematical examples, referencing the historical OUR/IM source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/3/7/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 lineage; no publisher artwork).

This lesson distinguishes its intended measurement, model and units. Work through the exact examples and explain how the representation supports each conclusion. For tasks requiring original construction, field measurements or open designs, a teacher must assess the artifact; a numeric verifier alone is insufficient.

Official OUR/IM 2017–2019 student task alignment: Counting Circle Grid Squares; Area Compared with Radius Squares. This lesson requires students to Use experimental area estimates to infer the constant relating circle area to radius squared. Equivalent first-party learner activity and its drawing/measurement evidence need teacher review; equations and visual tables are supporting representations only. Student source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/3/7/index.html.

KeyConcepts.Title: Grid area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Count full and partial unit squares inside a disk.
KeyConcepts.Example: A disk near 13 squares may have area about 13 units².

KeyConcepts.Title: Radius squared
KeyConcepts.Definition: Circle area scales with the square of radius.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A grows by factor k² when r grows by k.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling r quadruples area.

KeyConcepts.Title: π comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Disk area is a little more than three squares of side r.
KeyConcepts.Example: For r=2, area≈12.57.

WorkedExamples.Title: Circle area estimate
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate area of a disk with radius 2 using π≈3.14.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Slightly above 3r²=12.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove not proportional to diameter
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare areas for circles with radii 2 and 4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Area is not proportional to diameter.
WorkedExamples.Check: A/d ratios are π and 2π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare to square
WorkedExamples.Question: A radius-3 circle is placed inside a 6-by-6 square. What fraction of square area is the circle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Disk fits inside the square.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Counting Circle Grid Squares
WorkedExamples.Question: A circular paper disk of radius 4 cm is placed on a 1 cm grid. A careful count suggests about 50 square units inside. Use that result to estimate A/r², then predict an approximate area for a similar disk of radius 8 cm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Square the original radius: r²=4²=16 cm².
A doubled radius has four times the area, so predicted area≈50×4=200 cm².
Describe edge partial-squares and counting uncertainty; compare with 64π≈201.1 cm² as a check, not a substituted measurement.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Estimated area/r²≈3.125; doubled-radius disk around 200 cm².
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks actual grid counting or a faithfully annotated grid representation and the distinction from circumference scaling.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using C=πd for area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Circumference measures length, not surface covered.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use r² when finding area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling area directly proportional to radius
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Doubling radius quadruples area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use squared scale factors.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking a computed number alone as proof of a completed source lesson's physical measurement, diagram, group comparison or design task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher lesson requires original mathematical representations, observations or defended construction choices beyond a scalar answer.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the appropriate teacher rubric for the drawing or investigation and treat formula-based auto-marking only as supplementary practice.

SummaryPoints: A grows by factor k² when r grows by k.

Visuals.Title: Radius, diameter and circle area
Visuals.Description: Circle area is πr², so doubling radius multiplies area by four. Independently authored accessible comparison table with labeled rows and no publisher image.

Lessons.Title: Relating Area to Circumference
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Explain the circle-area formula through informal dissection into near-parallelograms or triangles. First-party mathematical examples, referencing the historical OUR/IM source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/3/8/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 lineage; no publisher artwork).

This lesson distinguishes its intended measurement, model and units. Work through the exact examples and explain how the representation supports each conclusion. For tasks requiring original construction, field measurements or open designs, a teacher must assess the artifact; a numeric verifier alone is insufficient.

Official OUR/IM 2017–2019 student task alignment: Rearranging Circular Sectors; Deriving the Circle Formula. This lesson requires students to Reassemble cut radial sectors into a near-parallelogram and justify its approximate base and height. Equivalent first-party learner activity and its drawing/measurement evidence need teacher review; equations and visual tables are supporting representations only. Student source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/3/8/index.html.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rearranged sectors
KeyConcepts.Definition: A circle cut into many sectors can approximate a parallelogram.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Base tends toward half-circumference; height tends toward radius.
KeyConcepts.Example: Base≈πr, height≈r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Half-circumference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Half of 2πr is πr.
KeyConcepts.Example: For r=3, half-circumference=3π.

KeyConcepts.Title: Derive area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rearranging preserves area in the limit.
KeyConcepts.Example: r=3 gives 9π.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find derived area
WorkedExamples.Question: Rearranged sectors approximate base πr and height r. Find area at r=5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Matches A=πr².

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare circumference and area
WorkedExamples.Question: If radius increases from 2 to 6, how do circumference and area change?
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: One measure is length; the other is area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain triangle dissection
WorkedExamples.Question: If the sectors rearrange into an approximate triangle with base 2πr and height r, find its area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Select the circle measurement required, perform the exact calculation and verify the geometric units.
WorkedExamples.Check: The conceptual limit requires increasingly thin sectors.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Rearranging Circular Sectors
WorkedExamples.Question: Cut an original radius-5 cm paper circle into 12 equal sectors and arrange them alternately point-up and point-down. Estimate the resulting near-parallelogram's base and height and infer the circle area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Mark 12 equal angular sectors and cut or draw all pieces without missing area.
Alternate orientations; the near-parallelogram's long edge approaches half the circumference, πr=5π cm.
Its height is close to the radius, 5 cm.
Thus rearranged area approaches base×height=(5π)(5)=25π cm²; show why more sectors smooth the sloped edge.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Area about 25π cm², justified by a sector rearrangement with base≈5π and height≈5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher inspects the original rearrangement diagram or physical sector model and the limiting-shape explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a few sectors form an exact parallelogram
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The construction is an approximation improving with more sectors.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe it as an informal limiting argument.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using circumference as full parallelogram base without adjustment
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The combined straight edge is half the circumference.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use C/2 as the base.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact disk area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Disk area is π times radius squared.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial disks
KeyConcepts.Definition: A semicircle has half the area of its full circle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Four Equal Circles in a Square
WorkedExamples.Question: Three original 10 cm-square designs contain respectively 1,4 and 9 equal circles arranged in a 1×1,2×2 or 3×3 packing, each touching cell sides. Calculate the total disk area in each design and the remaining uncovered area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: For 1 disk, radius=5 cm, total circle area=25π cm².
For 4 disks, each radius=2.5 cm, total=4×6.25π=25π cm².
For 9 disks, each radius=5/3 cm, total=9×(25/9)π=25π cm².
Uncovered square area is always 100−25π cm²; draw the three distinct arrangements.
WorkedExamples.Answer: All three layouts cover 25π cm² and leave 100−25π cm² uncovered.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher assesses 1-,4-,9-circle drawings, touching boundaries, radii and shaded-region reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Circumference or Area Poster
WorkedExamples.Question: A circular pond is 6 m across. A gardener needs an outer fence and a waterproof circular cover. Another pupil claims both require 6π because the diameter is 6. What measurements and units does each need?
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: The diameter is 6 m, so radius is 3 m.
Fence length is the circumference C=πd=6π m.
Cover material is the area A=πr²=9π m².
Create a two-column labeled diagram or poster; explain that linear and squared units prevent the formulas from being interchangeable.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Fence: 6π m. Cover: 9π m². The pupil's shared numerical formula is incorrect for area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher grades the original poster/diagram, dimensional argument and criticism of the false claim.

KeyConcepts.Title: Material cost model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Glass is priced per area while edging is priced per boundary length.
KeyConcepts.Example: Glass $2/m² and edge $3/m use different dimensional rates.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scaling price
KeyConcepts.Definition: When scaling by k, area costs change by k² while boundary costs change by k.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling dimensions quadruples glass cost but doubles edging cost.

KeyConcepts.Title: Human-reviewed design
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different valid windows can satisfy the same budget.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check geometry, cost assumptions, layout and explanation.
KeyConcepts.Example: Teacher reviews an original proposal, not one numeric target.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-task analogue — Window Costs
WorkedExamples.Question: Design an original rectangular stained-glass window 2 ft by 3 ft with a central clear circular region of radius 0.5 ft. Colored glass costs $5/ft², clear $2/ft², exterior frame $4/ft and circular separator $0.10/ft. Calculate total cost, and explain what changes at scale factor 2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Create the authentic student measurement/drawing/data representation first; explain the model, justify the mathematics and have a teacher review the artifact.
Steps: Total rectangle area is 6 ft²; the clear disk area is π(0.5)²=π/4 ft², and colored area is 6−π/4 ft².
Original outer frame perimeter is 10 ft; central circular separator length is π ft.
At scale factor 2, glass areas quadruple and frame/seam lengths double. Total cost becomes 4×(30−0.75π)+2×(40+0.10π)=200−2.8π dollars, about $191.20.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Original cost 70−0.65π≈$67.96; scaled version 200−2.8π≈$191.20, before labor/tax.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the labeled original colored/clear window design, units, non-overlap and budget assumptions; no number alone completes the design project.
